questions.prompt: After Chapter 11 concentrates force, what question does Chapter 12 add?
choices: Whether growth preserves or weakens that force
Whether every priority should get equal backing
Whether strategy should avoid all expansion
questions.explanation: Chapter 12 asks how expansion should be judged once focus has already concentrated effort.

choices: As an automatic sign of success
As a strategic outcome that must be judged
As something strategy should always resist
questions.explanation: The chapter rejects both automatic praise and automatic suspicion. Growth has to survive strategic judgment.

questions.prompt: Which mistake does the chapter criticize most directly?
choices: Thinking larger scale is automatically stronger strategy
Checking whether growth fits the current position
Refusing an expansion move that adds too much burden
questions.explanation: The target mistake is automatic-growth thinking, where size is treated as self-justifying.

questions.prompt: A school club wants many more members, but training and coordination are already strained. What is the Chapter 12 test?
choices: Whether the bigger roster looks more impressive
Whether the club can absorb the extra burden without losing force
Whether all expansion should be avoided on principle
questions.explanation: The right test is strategic fit under cost and constraint, not prestige or blanket anti-growth caution.

questions.prompt: Why do costs and constraints matter in growth decisions?
choices: Because they are part of what growth means strategically
Because they only appear after the strategy is already safe
Because they can be ignored when the opportunity looks large
questions.explanation: Growth is not just added size. It includes the burdens, coordination demands, and limits that arrive with the expansion.

choices: By replacing focus with generic ambition
By asking whether later enlargement preserves concentrated force
By treating diffusion as useful once growth begins
questions.explanation: Chapter 11 concentrates force; Chapter 12 tests whether expansion keeps that concentration meaningful.

questions.prompt: A side project grows so much that upkeep consumes the time that once made it good. Which concept fits best?
choices: Healthy scale as automatic progress
Growth weakening the original source of strength
Evidence that more features always deepen strategy
questions.explanation: The project becomes larger but strategically weaker because the added burden dissolves the force it once had.

questions.prompt: What is the best sign that growth is damaging strategy?
choices: Expansion widens scope while eroding focus and increasing burdens
A selective move reinforces the current source of strength
Scale is added without any new complexity
questions.explanation: Bad growth makes the organization broader, busier, and more burdened while weakening its strategic sharpness.

questions.prompt: Why can a larger organization still become strategically worse?
choices: Because growth always destroys strategy
Because extra scale can create coordination cost and softer force
Because strategy requires staying permanently small
questions.explanation: Chapter 12 warns that bigger can be broader yet blunter if the added scale stretches attention and coordination too far.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter point toward later discussions of dynamics and timing?
choices: Because growth changes how the strategy moves and what burdens appear over time
Because timing becomes irrelevant once scale increases
Because later chapters abandon the question of selective judgment
questions.explanation: Once growth is seen as a strategic choice, later chapters can ask how movement through time creates openings, burdens, and traps.
